title: What is BFS (Breadth First Search): visit all neighbors first before going deeper (use a queue); like exploring a maze level by level.
keyPoints: BFS explores a graph ring by ring using a queue, visiting all nodes at distance d before distance d+1
The first time BFS reaches a node is by the shortest path in an unweighted graph
Two structures are required: a queue for processing order and a visited set to prevent cycles
Time is O(V + E) visiting each vertex and edge once; space can be O(V) for the queue on wide graphs
Store a parent pointer at discovery time to reconstruct the actual shortest path
BFS is the right tool for shortest unweighted paths; switch to Dijkstra when edges have weights

s1_definition.oneliner: BFS explores a graph ring by ring using a queue, so it finds the fewest-hops path first.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Breadth-First Search (BFS)** is a graph traversal that explores all vertices at the current distance before moving one step farther.
- **Queue** processes vertices in discovery order, enforcing the level-by-level expansion.
- **Visited set** prevents revisiting and stops cycles from causing infinite loops.
- **Shortest path** in an unweighted graph is guaranteed because BFS reaches each node by the fewest hops first.
- **Time** is O(V + E); **space** is O(V) for the queue and visited set.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the fraud team at the National Bank of India starting from Rajesh's account and asking who received money directly from him. Those are the first ring. Then they ask who those people sent money to: the second ring. They finish checking everyone one hop away before looking at anyone two hops away. This ripple-outward search, like dropping a stone in a pond and watching circles spread, is breadth-first search.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  BFS level-by-level expansion
  ==============================

  Graph:  A --- B --- D
          |         |
          C --- E ---+

  BFS from A:
  ┌────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Level 0: Queue=[A]            │
  │    Process A → enqueue B, C    │
  │  Level 1: Queue=[B, C]         │
  │    Process B → enqueue D       │
  │    Process C → enqueue E       │
  │  Level 2: Queue=[D, E]         │
  │    Process D → (no new)        │
  │    Process E → (D already seen)│
  │  Done.                         │
  └────────────────────────────────┘

  Queue mechanics:
  ┌────────┐    ┌────────┐    ┌────────┐
  │ Enqueue│───▶│ Process│───▶│ Enqueue│
  │ source │    │ front  │    │ new    │
  │        │    │ of Q   │    │ nbrs   │
  └────────┘    └────────┘    └────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Breadth-First Search explores a graph ring by ring, visiting every vertex at the current distance before moving one step farther. It uses a queue to process vertices in discovery order and a visited set to prevent revisiting. Because it expands outward evenly, the first time BFS reaches any vertex is by the shortest path in an unweighted graph.

The mechanics are simple. Enqueue the source and mark it visited. Then loop: dequeue a vertex, process it, and for each unvisited neighbor, mark it and enqueue it. Marking at enqueue time rather than dequeue time is critical to avoid processing the same node multiple times. To reconstruct the actual shortest path, store a parent pointer at discovery time and trace back from the destination.

BFS is O(V + E) in time but can use O(V) memory because the queue may hold an entire level at once. It is the right tool for shortest paths in unweighted graphs and for finding everything within k hops. When edges have weights, switch to Dijkstra. When you only need reachability and memory is tight, DFS may be leaner.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used BFS in fraud analysis. Starting from a suspect account, the team wanted every account reachable through transfer chains and how many hops away each one was, because a wide reach in few hops suggests a mule network.

Remember one sentence: BFS uses a queue to explore level by level, so the first arrival at any node is the shortest unweighted path.
